html:
A nonviolent campaign from March 1924 to November 1925 at Vaikom, in the princely state of Travancore (now Kerala), to open the public roads around the Shiva temple to people of the lowest castes.

Travancore had some of the harshest caste rules in India. Ezhavas and Dalits could not use the roads near the temple, let alone enter it. Leaders of the Indian National Congress in Kerala, among them T. K. Madhavan and K. Kelappan, led volunteers of mixed castes to walk the roads every day. Police stopped them, and they were arrested in relays. During the monsoon floods the volunteers stood in neck-deep water and kept their protest. The reformer Narayana Guru backed them.

From Tamil country came E. V. Ramasamy, later known as Periyar, who was jailed and hailed as the "Vaikom hero". Gandhi visited and negotiated. It ended in a compromise that opened three of the four roads. It was the first major campaign in India against untouchability using satyagraha, and it led to the Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936, which opened Travancore's temples to all Hindus.
sum: A nonviolent campaign from March 1924 to November 1925 at Vaikom, in the princely state of Travancore (now Kerala), to open the public roads around the Shiva temple to people of the lowest castes.
